newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl launches jobs initiative for east Germany.
newsitem.headline: Kohl launches jobs initiative for east Germany.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Thursday launched a "jobs pact" with trade unions and business to create 100,000 new jobs a year in the former communist east, still blighted by unemployment seven years after unification.
"This is an important day for the new (eastern) states and Berlin," Kohl told a news conference to launch the joint pact.
"This is a good signal for the development of east Germany, for the future of the whole of Germany as a place to do business and also a clear signal of readiness to cooperate."

Kohl, who promised east Germans an economy with "blossoming landscapes" after unification in 1990, is anxious to bolster their faith in his government in the face of 17 percent unemployment and weak economic growth.
"Many people in the east feel repelled, unjustly treated and like second class citizens," Dieter Schulte, head of the German Federation of Trade Unions told the news conference.
"The goal of all these measures is to improve and equalise living standards," he said.

The pact came a day after Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt launched a new investment support package for the east to offer specifically-targeted investment grants rather than the existing tax depreciation incentives which have often led to investments being seen as having dubious value.

The package would initially keep investment support at constant levels but Rexrodt said it would cost around half as much by scrapping generous tax write-offs now available to investors in the region.

Kohl said he was sure the package, set to cut the burden on the annual budget from a current 11 billion marks ($6.5 billion) to 5.7 billion marks in 1999 and then to 4.4 billion after 2002, conformed to European Union regulations.
But the investment package and jobs pact came as two economic institutes published downbeat reports predicting further economic stagnation in the east.

The Cologne-based German Economics Institute said east German firms, particularly in the building sector, did not see any forthcoming improvement in growth, employment or investment. The Munich Ifo economic research institute said firms in the east were less optimistic in April than in March.

The new jobs plan aims to bring unions, politicians and industry together to reach agreement on job creation measures, training and investment in a forum likely to be similar to the Kohl's pet "Alliance for Jobs" that collapsed amid acrimony between trade unions and the government just over a year ago.
The forum will meet twice a year to work on solutions to the east's economic woes and report on its progress.

Hans-Peter Stihl, president of the Federation of German Chambers of Industry and Commerce, said the initiative showed that business was recognising its mutual responsibility for boosting development in the east, where productivity is currently just 57 percent of the level in the west.

Stihl said industry's main goals were to stabilise investment at a level that allowed above-average growth, boost consumption in the east by 50 percent by 2000 and help trade and the development of new businesses. "These are ambitious targets but I am sure we will achieve them," he said.

Manfred Stolpe, premier of the eastern state of Brandenburg said the initiative was necessary because unemployment threatened social peace. "People doubt the seriousness of the declaration so we must make it binding," he said.
Kohl said training was one of the most important parts of the pact. "Up to 80 percent of the more than four million unemployed in Germany have little or no training," he said.

Wolfgang Thierse, deputy leader of the opposition Social Democrats said the jobs pact was a step in the right direction but criticised the government's investment package, saying it represented a significant cut in support.

"The government is further saving on development of the east at a time when the distance between east and west is increasing both economically and socially," he told Berlin radio. ($ = 1.695 German Marks)
